analysis|01-08|1959|Ο Κάστρο μπαίνει στην Αβάνα|Castro enters Havana|Fidel Castro's revolution had begun in 1956 and soon became the main opponent of the Batista regime. The rebels gained much of the countryside, while opposition in the cities grew as a result of the corruption and instability of the regime. By the end of 1958 Batista's position was extremely weak. Havana was the economic and political centre of the island, so the entry of the rebels carried great symbolic weight. // After Batista's departure at the beginning of January 1959, his army surrendered its positions without serious resistance. On 8 January Castro's forces entered Havana, to a great popular welcome. Castro addressed the public and gradually took full power in the country. The 26th of July Movement had many members in the cities, who helped to weaken the regime from within. // The entry into Havana marked the end of the previous political order and the beginning of a radical change. The new government carried out agrarian reforms, nationalisations and closer cooperation with the Soviet Union. The revolution left deep marks on Cuba and on its relations with the United States for decades. The success of the revolution inspired movements in other countries of Latin America, which changed the balance for years.

analysis|01-08|1959|Ο ντε Γκωλ πρόεδρος της Πέμπτης Δημοκρατίας|De Gaulle becomes president of the Fifth Republic|In 1958 France was in a deep political crisis, triggered by the Algerian War and the instability of the Fourth Republic. Frequent changes of government had weakened the institutions, while the military leadership in Algeria threatened uncontrolled actions. Charles de Gaulle, leader of Free France during the war, returned to power as a figure who could impose balance. De Gaulle had withdrawn from politics in 1946, since he disagreed with the functioning of the party institutions of the Fourth Republic. // A new constitution, which strengthened the executive power and the role of the president, was approved by referendum in the autumn of 1958. In early January 1959 de Gaulle took up the duties of president, marking the start of the Fifth Republic. The new structure gave the president wider powers than in the past. The referendum on the new constitution passed by a broad majority, as many citizens were asking for stability. // The Fifth Republic developed into a stable institutional framework, which with amendments remains in force today. De Gaulle promoted the independence of Algeria, which came about in 1962, and pursued an independent foreign policy. His period remains a central point of modern French history. The Fifth Republic gave France a framework with a stronger role for the president and more stable governments.

analysis|01-09|1822|«Μένω»: ο Πέτρος Α΄ ανοίγει τον δρόμο προς την ανεξαρτησία της Βραζιλίας|"I stay": Pedro I paves the way to Brazil's independence|In 1808, when Napoleonic troops invaded Portugal, the royal family moved to Rio de Janeiro. Brazil, which was a colony of Portugal, became the seat of the monarchy and acquired a special position. After the return of King John VI to Europe in 1821, the claims of Brazil to autonomy were strengthened. The Brazilian elite had interests that conflicted with the orders from Lisbon, and the prince turned towards them. // The Portuguese Cortes sought to restore Brazil to a subordinate position and demanded the return of Prince Pedro to Europe. On 9 January 1822 Pedro declared that he would stay in Brazil, with the well-known phrase "Fico", meaning "I stay". This decision was an act of open resistance to the orders from Lisbon. Pedro's decision was part of a careful strategy, which included cooperation with local elites. // A few months later, in September 1822, Pedro proclaimed the independence of Brazil and took the throne of the new empire. The transition took place with relatively little violence, compared with other Latin American countries. Pedro I abdicated in 1831, and Brazil remained an empire until 1889. This process allowed Brazil to keep its monarchical form for almost seventy years.

analysis|01-09|1861|Το Μισισιπή αποσπάται από την Ένωση|Mississippi secedes from the Union|After the election of Abraham Lincoln in November 1860, many Southern states believed that the federal government would restrict slavery. South Carolina had already left, and the Southern economy, based on plantations, depended heavily on slavery. The inhabitants of the region saw the political change as a threat to their way of life. South Carolina had withdrawn as early as December 1860, and its example influenced the other Southern states. // On 9 January 1861 the convention of the state of Mississippi voted to secede from the Union. The decision was part of a common strategy of the Southern states, which sought to form a separate confederacy. Mississippi was the second state to leave, after South Carolina. The state conventions were gathered with delegates who regarded slavery as necessary for the economy. // Secession led to the formation of the Confederacy, which a few months later found itself at war with the Union. The Civil War broke out in April 1861 with the battle at Fort Sumter. Mississippi, an important producer of cotton, became a scene of bloody clashes throughout the conflict. The difference between the North and the South over slavery and the rights of the states lay at the heart of the conflict.

analysis|01-09|1960|Αρχίζει το φράγμα του Ασσουάν|Construction of the Aswan Dam begins|For centuries the Nile was the basis of Egyptian agriculture, with the annual floods fertilising the fields. The floods, however, were uneven and sometimes disastrous, while population growth required more water for irrigation. The government of Gamal Abdel Nasser sought a solution in a large project to control the river. The project was one of the largest of its era in Africa and became a central point of Nasser's national policy. // Initially the funding came from Western countries, but in 1956 the United States and Britain withdrew from the project. The Soviet Union took over support for the project, and construction of the dam began in the early 1960s. The dam was completed later, forming Lake Nasser. The lake that was created covered large parts of Nubia, and thousands of people were resettled. // The dam regulated the floods, increased the production of electricity and extended the cultivable land. However, the retention of silt reduced the supply of nutrients to the Delta and affected fishing and agriculture. The project remains a subject of debate for its ecological and political results. The dam's energy today provides a significant part of Egypt's electricity production.

analysis|01-09|2007|Ο Στιβ Τζομπς παρουσιάζει το πρώτο iPhone|Steve Jobs presents the first iPhone|At the beginning of the twenty-first century mobile phones were mainly voice communication devices, with keypads and limited functions. Manufacturers tried to add internet access and applications, but the user experience was often difficult. The success of the iPod had already shown Apple the power of clean design and ease of use. Apple already had considerable experience in designing products with a focus on the user experience. // On 9 January 2007 Steve Jobs presented in San Francisco the device that combined a mobile phone, an iPod and internet access, with a touchscreen. The presentation became part of the history of technology. The device went on sale later that same year, and initial demand was high. The new device was initially released only in the United States, in cooperation with a major telephone company. // The iPhone changed expectations of the mobile phone, which was transformed from a simple telephone into a small computer in the pocket. The market for applications, which opened shortly afterwards, shaped new business models. The device gave impetus to a generation of mobile phones with touchscreens and deeply affected everyday digital life. The success of the device led many manufacturers to adopt similar designs with a touchscreen.

analysis|01-10|-49|Ο Καίσαρας περνά τον Ρουβίκωνα|Caesar crosses the Rubicon|In the first century BC the Roman Republic was plagued by rivalries among powerful generals. Caesar had commanded Roman forces in Gaul for years and had gained great popularity and wealth. The Senate, led by the conservatives, was worried about his growing power and demanded that he hand over command of the legions. The strong rivalries of the time had weakened the institutions of the Republic. // When Caesar refused, the Senate declared him an enemy of Rome. According to tradition, Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his troops, the river that separated Gaul from Italy, and spoke the phrase "the die is cast". Entering Italy with an army was considered open rebellion. This particular date is traditional and is not confirmed with certainty. The Rubicon was regarded as the boundary of Italy, and crossing it with an army meant violating the law of Rome. // The civil war that followed led to Caesar's victory over Pompey and to the concentration of power in his hands. In 44 BC Caesar was assassinated, but the Roman Republic had already effectively come to an end. In 27 BC the Roman Empire was founded, an event that shaped the history of the Mediterranean for centuries. The civil war changed the political system of Rome, and the old form of the Republic never fully returned.

analysis|01-10|1812|Το πρώτο ατμόπλοιο στον Μισσισσιππή φτάνει στη Νέα Ορλεάνη|The first steamboat reaches New Orleans on the Mississippi|At the beginning of the nineteenth century transport in the United States relied mainly on rivers and wooden craft, which moved with the current or with oars. The Mississippi was the main axis for sending goods from the interior towards the Gulf of Mexico, but upstream navigation was difficult. Engineers were trying to apply steam to navigation, following the successes of Robert Fulton on the rivers of the eastern side. The steamboats of the era needed large quantities of fuel and special construction to withstand the currents. // The steamboat New Orleans was built at Pittsburgh and travelled downstream on the Mississippi, reaching New Orleans in January 1812. The journey was long and difficult, with obstacles and adventures along the route. The arrival of the vessel was an important milestone for the technology of the era. The route from Pittsburgh, which lies in the upper Ohio, was particularly demanding for the pilot. // This success opened the way for the spread of steamboats on the Mississippi, which soon transformed commercial transport. Steamboats reduced the time and cost of transport, and the trade of the interior was strengthened. This development contributed to the economic growth of the region in the nineteenth century. With the spread of steamboats, the river became a common route for the population of the western states.

analysis|01-10|1901|Η πετρελαιοπηγή του Σπίντλτοπ στο Τέξας|The Spindletop oil gusher in Texas|At the end of the nineteenth century oil was used mainly for lighting and lubricants, while the internal combustion engine was still in its infancy. Geologists suspected that Texas hid deposits, but drilling was rare and very risky. The area near Beaumont had small signs of oil, which encouraged investment. The region was known for its geological formations, which supported the hypothesis that oil was present. // On 10 January 1901 the Spindletop well reached great depth and produced a gusher of oil with astonishing force, which shot high above the derrick. The phenomenon, known as a gusher, released an enormous quantity of oil over several days. The news spread quickly and attracted crowds of investors and workers to the area. Its production rose rapidly, and oil markets came under intense pressure for new drilling. // Spindletop opened the age of the oil industry in Texas and in the United States, with new wells, companies and the creation of new towns. The discovery dramatically increased production and strengthened the economic power of the state. Oil thus became the main fuel of the following era, with deep consequences for industry, transport and global politics. The discovery reshaped global energy, as oil began to compete with coal as the chief source of energy.

analysis|01-10|1920|Τίθεται σε ισχύ η Συνθήκη των Βερσαλλιών|The Treaty of Versailles takes effect|After the First World War the victorious powers gathered their representatives in Paris to shape the new European order. Germany, which had been defeated, did not take part in the negotiations and was asked to accept predetermined terms. The treaty was signed at Versailles in June 1919, with territorial losses, restrictions on the army and an obligation to pay reparations. The clause on responsibility for the war caused particular resentment among the German public. The treaty also included the creation of new states in Europe, such as Czechoslovakia and Poland, with borders different from the earlier ones. // The treaty formally came into force on 10 January 1920, the same day that the League of Nations began operating. The new organisation had been founded to guarantee peace, but it had no means of enforcement of its own. The United States did not ratify the treaty, a fact that weakened its worldwide application. Britain and France took on much of the management of European affairs. Germany lost its colonies and part of its territory, while its army was limited to a specific number of troops. // The treaty left deep resentment in Germany, which was later linked with the rise of extreme political forces. The economic coercion, through the pressure of reparations, contributed to the crises of the 1920s. Many historians regard its consequences as one of the causes of the Second World War. At the same time, the creation of new states in eastern Europe changed the map of the region for decades. The implementation of the terms was debated for years, and many decisions were renegotiated during the 1920s.

analysis|01-10|1946|Η πρώτη συνεδρίαση της Γενικής Συνέλευσης του ΟΗΕ|The first session of the UN General Assembly|The United Nations was founded by the Charter of San Francisco in 1945, after the destruction caused by the Second World War. The need for an international mechanism for dialogue was self-evident, particularly after the failure of the League of Nations. The representatives of the states had to find ways of cooperating in a world that had just emerged from the conflict. The session opened with the presence of representatives of many countries who wished to promote cooperation after the war. // The first session of the General Assembly took place in London in January 1946, in a city building that had been made available for the purpose. Representatives of fifty-one states took part, representing the members of the new organisation. The issues discussed concerned peace, disarmament and the humanitarian needs of populations. The seat of the organisation was later moved to New York, where its headquarters building stands today. // This conference laid the foundations for the functioning of the United Nations, with each state's vote equal in the General Assembly. The organisation later developed many bodies and specialised programmes. Today the General Assembly remains the best-known venue for multilateral dialogue in the world, although its decisions do not always have binding force. Its work later evolved through many peacekeeping operations in various parts of the world.

analysis|01-11|1922|Η πρώτη χρήση ινσουλίνης σε άνθρωπο|The first use of insulin in a human|Before the 1920s, type 1 diabetes was almost always a fatal disease, particularly for children and young people. Doctors knew that the deficiency of a substance in the body was responsible, but had no way of replacing it. A diagnosis usually meant a strict diet and little hope of survival. The discovery began with experiments on dogs, which showed that the pancreas produces a substance that regulates blood sugar. // In Toronto, the researchers Banting and Best managed to isolate insulin from animal pancreas in a university laboratory. The substance was tested first on dogs and then on humans, with care for the purity of the drug. In January 1922 it was given to a young diabetic, who was one of the first children to be saved with this treatment. The researchers worked with chemists and biochemists, so that the production and purity of the drug could be improved. // This success opened the way to the mass production of insulin across the world. In 1923 Banting and Macleod were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and research continued for better purity and dosing. Today insulin is a basic medicine for millions of people with diabetes, and the discovery is regarded as one of the great achievements of twentieth-century medicine. The treatment turned type 1 diabetes from a fatal disease into a chronic condition controlled by systematic treatment.

analysis|01-11|1923|Γαλλικά και βελγικά στρατεύματα μπαίνουν στη Ρουρ|French and Belgian troops enter the Ruhr|After the First World War, Germany owed reparations to France and Belgium under the terms of the Treaty of Versailles. The country's economy was exhausted, and payments were made late or not at all. The Ruhr region, with its coal mines and heavy industry, was a critical source of wealth. The French government believed that the delay in payments was deliberate and demanded guarantees for the debts of the war. // On 11 January 1923 French and Belgian troops entered the Ruhr, because Germany was delaying deliveries of coal and timber. The occupation met passive resistance from the workers, who avoided cooperating with the occupying forces. The Berlin government supported the workers with financial aid, which worsened the economy. The Ruhr was one of the most important industrial regions of Europe, with extensive steel production. // The occupation caused a severe hyperinflationary crisis in Germany and led to social upheaval. The German mark lost almost all its value within a few months. International diplomacy responded with the Dawes Plan of 1924, which regulated the payments, and the occupying forces withdrew in 1925. The episode is regarded as one of the points that revealed the limits of the peace settlement. The crisis was finally resolved by an international agreement that regulated the terms of payments and of withdrawal.

analysis|01-11|1935|Η Αμέλια Έρχαρτ πετά μόνη από τη Χαβάη στην Καλιφόρνια|Amelia Earhart flies solo from Hawaii to California|Aviation in the 1930s was in a phase of intense development, with pilots seeking new records for endurance and routes. The great sea routes, and especially the Pacific, were particularly demanding for the aircraft of the era. Earhart had already become famous for her flight across the Atlantic. The flight lasted several hours, and the aviator relied mainly on her calculations and on the aircraft's instruments. // On 11 January 1935 Amelia Earhart took off from Hawaii and landed in California, flying alone over the Pacific. The route required accuracy in navigation, since there were no easy landmarks over the ocean. The achievement was unprecedented, and the flight attracted great interest from the media. Earhart had already become known for the record of crossing the Atlantic as the sole pilot in 1932. // The feat enhanced Earhart's reputation as a pioneer of aviation and as a symbol of women's independence. A few years later, in 1937, she attempted a round-the-world flight and disappeared over the Pacific. Her story continues to move people, and her route remains an example of bold pioneering. The round-the-world flight she attempted in 1937 was part of an ambitious plan that was never completed.

analysis|01-11|1946|Ανακηρύσσεται η Λαϊκή Δημοκρατία της Αλβανίας|The People's Republic of Albania is proclaimed|Albania was placed under Italian occupation in 1939, and later under German occupation during the Second World War. During the occupation a strong resistance movement developed, dominated by the Communist Party. This leadership was well organised and had the support of part of the population. The decision coincided with the change in the political landscape of the Balkans and with the need to organise a new state. // In early 1946 the constituent assembly of the country voted to abolish the monarchy and proclaim a People's Republic, led by Enver Hoxha. The decision was taken under the influence of the political system that had prevailed after the war in the region. The new state began to organise the administration and the economy through state planning. King Zog had already left the country during the war, and the monarchy no longer had any real function. // The regime that followed was Stalinist, with strict control of power and restriction of freedoms. Albania was gradually isolated from most countries, even from the Soviet Union in the 1960s. The regime lasted until 1990, and this period left deep marks on the society and economy of the country. Power was to a large extent confined to the party, which controlled political life until the final years of the century.

analysis|01-11|1964|Η πρώτη έκθεση για τις βλάβες του καπνίσματος|The first report on the harms of smoking|In the 1950s and 1960s cases of lung cancer had increased considerably in the United States and in other countries. Epidemiological studies had linked smoking with these diseases, but public opinion was divided and the tobacco industry disputed the evidence. The need for an official assessment had become pressing. The report evaluated hundreds of studies and linked smoking with several serious diseases, not only with lung cancer. // On 11 January 1964 the US Surgeon General, Luther Terry, published a report that gathered the evidence from research and concluded that smoking causes lung cancer. The finding was official and well documented, with an extensive analysis of the scientific data. The report immediately became a key point of reference in public debate. The tobacco industry had for years opposed the results of the research, and the public reaction was intense. // The official recognition of the risks led to the adoption of warning labels on cigarette packets from the following year, under the law on the labelling of tobacco products. The public campaign against smoking was strengthened and in the following years many legislative interventions followed. This report is regarded as a milestone for medical prevention and the protection of public health. The report prompted similar studies in other countries and changes in international public health policy.

analysis|01-12|1932|Η Χάτι Κάραγουεϊ γίνεται η πρώτη γυναίκα γερουσιαστής|Hattie Caraway becomes the first woman senator|After women were granted the right to vote in 1920, the United States still had very few women in the highest offices. The Senate was a body where the participation of women was rare, and the idea of a woman senator was regarded by many as unusual. State elections, however, began to open new paths. Her entry into the Senate coincided with a time when Congress had very few women members, and their presence was unprecedented. // Hattie Caraway had succeeded her husband, the senator from Arkansas, after his death in 1931, and was temporarily appointed to his seat. She then stood in a special election and won, which meant she entered the Senate for a full term. Taking up her duties was historic, since she was the first woman elected to this office. Her presence in the Senate was modest but steady, and she approached politics with a careful attitude. // Her election opened the way for other women in the political life of the country. She continued in office, was re-elected and served until 1945. Her term is a landmark for the participation of women in the American Congress and in the political institutional processes of the era. Her case helped create a precedent for the women who followed in the legislative power.

analysis|01-12|1991|Το Κογκρέσο εγκρίνει τη χρήση βίας στον Κόλπο|Congress approves the use of force in the Gulf|In August 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait, a small but oil-rich state in the Persian Gulf. The UN Security Council imposed economic sanctions and set a deadline for the withdrawal of Iraqi troops. The crisis raised concern for the security of oil supplies in the world market. The authorisation decision was one of the rare occasions on which Congress voted such an authorisation before a conflict. // In January 1991 the US Congress voted to authorise the use of military force, if Iraq did not withdraw from Kuwait. The decision was narrowly voted, and it marked the agreement of domestic politics on military intervention. The international coalition of forces was already preparing in the region. The campaign rested on a broad international coalition, with the participation of many Arab and European states. // The authorisation paved the way for the war to liberate Kuwait, which began a few days later with air attacks. The campaign was completed with the withdrawal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait in February 1991. The conflict left political and humanitarian consequences, and the region remained in a state of tension for years. The conflict left deep consequences for the economy of the region and for international diplomacy.

analysis|01-12|2010|Καταστροφικός σεισμός στην Αϊτή|Devastating earthquake in Haiti|Haiti was among the poorest countries in the Western Hemisphere, with severe poverty and weak public infrastructure. The capital, Port-au-Prince, had grown densely, with many buildings that did not strictly follow earthquake-resistant standards. Seismologists knew that the area lies close to active faults. The disaster affected a large part of the population, with millions of people needing immediate help with food, water and shelter. // On 12 January 2010 an earthquake of magnitude 7 on the Richter scale struck the island, with its epicentre close to the capital. Thousands of buildings collapsed, and many services, such as hospitals and government offices, were destroyed. Estimates of the dead exceeded one hundred thousand, although the exact figures remain uncertain. Many international organisations and governments sent rescue teams and medical staff to the area. // International aid was mobilised immediately, with the gathering of humanitarian missions and funding. Reconstruction, however, proceeded slowly, and in the months that followed a cholera epidemic broke out. The disaster once again brought to the forefront the question of earthquake codes and the resilience of poor countries. The reconstruction of the country was linked to discussions about the need for long-term development and institutional strengthening. This historic event continues to be studied by researchers and historians around the world. The sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events.

analysis|01-13|1898|Το «Κατηγορώ» του Εμίλ Ζολά|Zola's "J'accuse"|The Dreyfus affair began in 1894, when a Jewish officer of the French army was convicted of espionage. The conviction was based on doubtful evidence and developed into a fierce social dispute, with the expression of antisemitic feelings. The military leadership refused to review the decision. Zola's text was written in a clear and dramatic style, and contained specific accusations against the people involved. // On 13 January 1898 the writer Émile Zola published in the newspaper L'Aurore an open letter to the President of the Republic, under the title "J'accuse". The text named army officers and accused them of cover-up, and condemned the conviction of an innocent man. The publication provoked an enormous confrontation in French public opinion. Zola's trial gave rise to new waves of debate about freedom of the press and justice. // Zola was tried for defamation and convicted, and was forced to flee to England. Dreyfus was later cleared and returned to the army, with official rehabilitation in 1906. The affair remains in history as a symbol of the defence of individual rights and of the political responsibility of intellectuals. The affair left its mark on the history of French law and on the shaping of modern intellectual life. The sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events.

analysis|01-13|1999|Ο Μάικλ Τζόρνταν αποσύρεται|Michael Jordan retires|Michael Jordan was the leading basketball player of the 1990s, with the Chicago Bulls winning six NBA championships. The team had built a dynastic cycle of success, combining individual quality with collective work. His career had become a global phenomenon, with great commercial success. The Chicago team had already begun to change its line-up before his departure, with new players in the key positions. // In January 1999 Jordan announced that he was retiring from basketball, for a second time after his first retirement in 1993. His decision coincided with the change of era for the team and for the league. The news became widely known and provoked great discussion about the future of the team. The team's supporters were to a large extent grateful for the years of titles he had given them. // Jordan's departure ended one of the most brilliant chapters of American sport. He later returned to the game with other teams, without however repeating the earlier dynasty. His presence remains a reference point for sport and for the spread of basketball around the world. His relationship with the NBA remained strong, and his figure remains central to the history of the sport.

analysis|01-14|1900|Πρεμιέρα της «Τόσκα»|Premiere of Tosca|At the end of the nineteenth century Italian opera was moving towards verismo, a current that sought realistic plots, passions and everyday life. Giacomo Puccini was one of the main representatives of this direction, and his collaboration with librettists was close. The audiences of Rome and Milan sought new works that combined emotion and spectacle. Puccini composed the work with particular care for its drama and its orchestral writing. // On 14 January 1900 the opera "Tosca" was presented in Rome, at the Teatro Costanzi, based on the play by the Frenchman Victorien Sardou. The plot contained political and romantic conflicts, with dramatic scenes and well-known arias. The performance provoked enthusiasm, although the critics were divided over its originality. The story unfolds in Rome in 1800 and has a strong political background. // Tosca soon became one of the most popular works in the repertoire and remains one of the most performed operas. Its success strengthened Puccini's reputation, and he later wrote other classic works. The work is an example of the power of melodrama on the modern stage. The opera is performed today on major stages around the world and is a constant element of the repertoire.

analysis|01-14|1907|Καταστροφικός σεισμός στο Κίνγκστον|Devastating earthquake in Kingston|Jamaica was a British colony at the beginning of the twentieth century, with Kingston as its main port and capital. The city had grown quickly, with buildings that were not always resistant to earthquakes. The area was known for its seismic activity, which however had not been studied in great detail. The earthquake occurred at a time when building techniques were not yet adapted to the seismic demands of the region. // On 14 January 1907 a powerful earthquake struck Kingston and the surrounding areas, causing the collapse of many buildings. The fires that followed worsened the disaster, as the wooden houses burned quickly. Around a thousand people were killed, and many were left homeless. Help for the affected came from other British territories and from communities in the Caribbean and America. // The disaster led to the rebuilding of the city under stricter rules, which included better materials and safety standards. This experience contributed to the study of seismic hazard in the Caribbean. Today Kingston remains one of the most important cities in the region, and the memory of the disaster reminds us of the value of prevention. The reconstruction followed gradually, and the city returned to functioning after several years.

analysis|01-15|1759|Ανοίγει το Βρετανικό Μουσείο|The British Museum opens|In the eighteenth century Britain experienced great intellectual development, with collections that sought the ideas of the Enlightenment. The physician and naturalist Hans Sloane had gathered a large collection of objects, books and natural specimens. After his death, Parliament purchased the collection so that it would be public and accessible. The Sloane collection included objects from many parts of the world and formed the core of the first exhibits. // The British Museum opened on 15 January 1759 in London, in the Montagu House building, and it was the first national museum to be offered to the public. Admission was free, which was unusual for the time. Visitors could see collections of natural history, objects and books. The museum developed later with many donations and acquisitions, which greatly increased the collection. // The museum became a model for many national museums around the world and contributed to the spread of knowledge among wider social groups. Over the years the collection expanded considerably and the building was moved to new premises. Today the British Museum remains one of the most visited museums in the world and a point of reference for cultural heritage. Today admission to the permanent collections remains free, which has become a hallmark of the museum.

analysis|01-15|1919|Δολοφονείται η Ρόζα Λούξεμπουργκ|Rosa Luxemburg is murdered|After Germany's defeat in 1918 the country fell into deep political turmoil, with workers' uprisings and political conflicts. Rosa Luxemburg, together with Karl Liebknecht, was among the central figures of the left wing of the German Social Democratic Party. The two leaders supported revolutionary change and opposed the agreement with the government. The murder took place within the chaos of the era, while the forces of order intensified the suppression of the uprisings. // In January 1919 the Spartacist uprising broke out in Berlin, which was suppressed with military forces. On 15 January Luxemburg and Liebknecht were arrested and murdered by a group of officers while they were being transported. The murder provoked a strong reaction on the left. Luxemburg's body was later found in a canal, and the case caused great outrage. // The murder of Luxemburg left a deep wound in the German workers' movement and in the political life of the Weimar period. It was a symbol of the violent suppression of opponents of power in post-war Germany. Her memory remains strong in the history of the left, and commemorative events are held every year. Most of the people who took part were not prosecuted immediately, which strengthened the distrust of the left.

analysis|01-15|1970|Η Μπιάφρα παραδίνεται|Biafra surrenders|Nigeria was a country with intense ethnic and religious differences, among the Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo populations. In 1967 the eastern region, with an Igbo majority, declared its independence as the Republic of Biafra. The reaction of the central government was immediate and harsh, and the conflict developed into war. Famine and blockade created a humanitarian crisis that drew the attention of international public opinion. // The war was accompanied by famine and a humanitarian crisis, with estimates of the dead from hunger ranging in the hundreds of thousands. The isolation of the region made it difficult for aid to enter, and the world's media covered the images of the famine. In January 1970 the Biafran forces laid down their arms. International organisations carried out relief operations, with limited access to the affected areas. // The surrender brought an end to the civil war, and Nigeria moved towards political reunification with the aim of reconciliation. The crisis left deep wounds in the country, with long-term consequences for social balance. The war of Biafra remains a point of reference for humanitarian aid and for the issues of national self-determination. The conflict left behind questions about the limits of humanitarian intervention and the fate of civilians.

analysis|01-15|2001|Ξεκινά η Βικιπαίδεια|Wikipedia begins|The idea of collaborative knowledge had developed in the wider online environment before Wikipedia, with open communities and tools for cooperation. Academic circles were sceptical of an encyclopaedia without strict expert review. The need for access to information in many languages was growing ever stronger.
